disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Inattentive Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of difficulties with sustained focus, organization, and follow-through that are developmentally inappropriate and cause functional impairment across settings. Individuals typically show at least six inattentive symptoms for at least six months, with minimal or no prominent hyperactive-impulsive features, and symptoms must have been present since childhood even if they only become impairing under increased demands in adolescence or adulthood. The clinical course is often chronic, with fluctuating severity that becomes more evident when academic, occupational, or multitasking demands increase, such as during school transitions, job promotions, or major life changes. It is distinguished from anxiety, depression, or situational stress by the early onset, pervasiveness across contexts, and a longstanding history of organizational and attention difficulties rather than problems emerging solely in response to a discrete stressor.

narrative.personality: Paul is a pragmatic, competitive, and socially energetic outdoors enthusiast who enjoys hands-on work, new tech, and mentoring others in a structured but laid-back style.
narrative.stressor: About two and a half years ago, Paul was moved from being a field technician to a crew supervisor-in-training, which suddenly shifted his work from mostly physical tasks to a heavier load of planning, coordinating materials, and keeping track of multiple job sites and schedules. Responsibilities like tracking equipment, managing smart-irrigation controllers, and juggling bids and budgets exposed long-standing attention and organization difficulties that he had previously compensated for with his strong work ethic, physical energy, and hands-on skills. Over the next two years, small but frequent mix-ups with tools, project plans, and paperwork began to strain relationships with his boss and crew, leading to missed opportunities for promotion and growing self-doubt, despite him spending more time trying to “get organized.” After a particularly embarrassing incident where misplaced equipment delayed a major eco-focused project and he was formally written up, Paul became worried that his career trajectory was stalling and agreed to seek a psychiatric evaluation at the urging of his manager and a close friend.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep misplacing tools, paperwork, and my gear at work, and it’s starting to get me in trouble.”

narrative.personality: Abel is a calm, confident, and socially skilled sales leader who is methodical with numbers yet spontaneous and passionate in his family life, cooking, and salsa dancing.
narrative.stressor: Roughly two and a half years ago, Abel’s company merged with another firm, increasing his territory and forcing him to manage more client relationships while also spending more evenings on the road or on calls. At the same time, his children were entering school-age and his wife began asking for more shared decision-making at home, leading to frequent conversations about schedules, finances, and parenting that required his full attention after long workdays. Under this combined pressure, his lifelong tendency to mentally drift during conversations became increasingly problematic, with his wife feeling ignored and his team complaining that he seemed disengaged or missed key points in one-on-one meetings, despite his strong performance metrics. After a series of escalating arguments at home over him “not listening” to important discussions about the kids and a near-loss of a major account when he overlooked client concerns raised in a meeting, Abel grew concerned that something beyond stress was affecting him and sought psychiatric care to understand what was going on.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My wife and my team keep saying I’m not listening to them, even when I’m really trying to pay attention.”

narrative.personality: Mildrey is a laid-back, curious, and creatively driven young professional who connects warmly with clients while following her artistic interests in photography, sketching, and culture.
narrative.stressor: Around two years and four months ago, Mildrey transitioned from being a college student with a flexible schedule into full-time real estate work, where success depended on managing multiple listings, deadlines, and extensive paperwork. While she excelled at the creative and interpersonal aspects—staging homes, photographing properties, and building rapport—she found the less stimulating parts of the job, such as contract details, documentation, and long training modules, increasingly difficult to consistently tackle. Over time, her relaxed approach and longstanding tendency to procrastinate on mentally draining tasks led to missed opportunities, delayed follow-ups, and gentle reprimands from her broker for incomplete files, threatening her income and reputation. After noticing that she repeatedly fell behind on licensing coursework, continuing education, and meticulous client documentation despite genuine interest in the field, Mildrey became frustrated with herself and sought a psychiatric evaluation to understand why she struggled so much with the sustained mental effort her new role required.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Whenever there’s paperwork or anything that takes a lot of mental focus, I just can’t seem to make myself stick with it.”
